short: Czechoslovakia's border defences signed away at a conference it was not invited to.
full:
Hitler demanded the Sudetenland, the German-speaking border region of Czechoslovakia, which also held the country's frontier fortifications and much of its heavy industry. After two inconclusive meetings, Chamberlain, Daladier, Mussolini and Hitler met in Munich on 29 September 1938 and signed in the early hours of the 30th. The Czechoslovak government, which had not been invited, was told to accept. Chamberlain returned to Heston aerodrome with a separate declaration of Anglo-German friendship and spoke of peace for our time.

The agreement was popular at the time. A European war appeared to have been avoided, and Britain used the year it bought to build radar stations and Hurricane and Spitfire squadrons. But Czechoslovakia lost its defences and some 70 per cent of its heavy industry, and German troops occupied Prague on 15 March 1939 in open breach of the terms. Britain then guaranteed Poland. Munich has served ever since as the standard argument against conceding to a dictator's demands.
